findings.title: No authentication/authorization on any endpoint (incl. network-position trust)
findings.attack_path: Anonymous client issues GET http://<server-alb>/api/getAllProducts (or /api/docs) with no credential and no control to bypass; every route is unauthenticated. Absorbs the zero-trust/network-position gap (former TM-009): tasks authorize inbound purely by ALB source-SG with no per-request identity, but the fronting ALB is itself Internet-facing, so anything it forwards is implicitly trusted. Root access-control gap that also leaves any future privileged route unprotected by construction and removes the natural throttle/attribution for the abuse findings.
findings.remediation: Introduce request-level authentication (e.g., ALB OIDC/Cognito, an API gateway with keys/JWT, or mTLS) on both ALBs and, at minimum, on the API; enforce per-request authorization rather than trust-by-network-position. Even for a demo, gate the API behind an auth check so the abuse and future-privileged-route risks are contained.

findings.title: Cleartext HTTP on both public ALBs (no TLS) — transit interception & response tampering
findings.attack_path: On-path attacker (rogue Wi-Fi / ISP / compromised transit) between the browser and the public ALBs reads all request/response traffic and injects a modified HTTP response (replace the SPA bundle or API JSON) served to the victim's browser. Only an http_listener:80 is instantiated; the https_listener resource exists but is gated behind var.enable_https (default false, never set). No HSTS, no redirect. ALB->task hop is also plaintext.
findings.remediation: Set enable_https=true, attach an ACM certificate, add an HTTP->HTTPS 301 redirect and HSTS; terminate TLS at the ALB and use HTTPS to the task or keep it inside the VPC. The HTTPS listener already exists in the module, so this is a low-effort flip of an existing flag plus a cert.

findings.title: Swagger / OpenAPI UI publicly reachable (/api/docs) — attack-surface enumeration
findings.attack_path: GET /api/docs (the URL is published in the Terraform output) returns the anonymous Swagger UI and machine-readable spec, handing an attacker the full API contract for enumeration. Low intrinsic secrecy today (3 trivial routes) but the blast radius grows silently as the API grows.
findings.remediation: Do not expose Swagger UI/spec on the public API in production: gate it behind auth, bind it to an internal-only path, or disable it in the deployed image. Keep API docs out of the public Terraform output.

findings.title: No WAF / rate limiting / bot control in front of public ALBs — L7 DoS & scraping
findings.attack_path: A single host floods or scrapes either ALB with no upstream throttle; autoscaling is capped (min 1 / max 4 tasks), so saturation is reached quickly and there is no L7 shield to absorb it.
findings.remediation: Attach AWS WAF (rate-based rules, bot control, IP reputation) to both ALBs; add per-client rate limiting and request quotas; consider a higher autoscaling ceiling or a CDN/edge shield for the static SPA.

findings.title: Unauthenticated full-table scan on every request -> cost amplification / economic DoS
findings.attack_path: /api/getAllProducts issues a full-table DynamoDB scan per call on a PAY_PER_REQUEST table. With no auth (TM-001) and no rate limit (TM-004), an attacker loops the endpoint to drive unbounded read-capacity + data-transfer billing and to exhaust the 4-task ceiling — availability and direct financial impact from a trivial script.
findings.remediation: Replace the unbounded scan with a paginated Query on an indexed access pattern; add caching (e.g., CloudFront/ElastiCache) in front of the read; enforce rate limits and auth (TM-001/TM-004); set DynamoDB/billing alarms and budget guardrails.

findings.title: Permissive CORS (cors() reflects any origin)
findings.attack_path: app.use(cors()) reflects any Origin, so any website can read API responses from a visitor's browser. Impact bounded today — responses carry no credentials/cookies and the data is already anonymous/public — but becomes serious the moment auth or cookies are introduced.
findings.remediation: Configure an explicit CORS origin allowlist scoped to the SPA's known origin(s); do not reflect arbitrary origins. Re-tighten immediately if any authenticated/cookie-bearing endpoint is added.

findings.title: Error-message information disclosure to client
findings.attack_path: Both the inline scan handler and the error middleware return err.message (and err.status) to the caller. Inducing a backend error (throttle/permission/timeout) leaks AWS SDK internal detail — table name, region, ARNs, throttling/permission specifics — that aids reconnaissance.
findings.remediation: Return generic client-facing error messages with a correlation id; log the detailed error server-side only. Never surface raw SDK error text or status to the client.

findings.title: Fragile error handling on the API error path
findings.attack_path: The scan-error branch is handled inline (res.send -> HTTP 200 with code: undefined) — malformed but does not throw. The error middleware's res.status(error.code) throws a RangeError only for a status-less error routed through it, and the stray 'status: err.status || 500' is a dead JS label. A real robustness defect (malformed error responses, brittle degradation) but the unhandled-exception path is largely theoretical for the SDK scan flow.
findings.remediation: Normalize errors through a single handler: coerce to a valid HTTP status (default 500), remove the dead label, declare AB3_TABLE with const, and return a consistent error body. Add a test that drives the SDK error path.

findings.title: ECS task role carries iam:PassRole on * — latent privilege escalation
findings.attack_path: The application runtime identity (ECS task role R2) holds iam:PassRole on every role in the account (IAM/main.tf:317-323). An attacker who compromises the server container inherits the task role and can pass any role to a reachable service action — the classic PassRole escalation primitive — unnecessary for a read-only catalog API.
findings.remediation: Remove the iam:PassRole statement from the task role entirely (the runtime app does not need it) — a one-statement deletion. Keep only the scoped DynamoDB-read and S3-GetObject grants.

findings.title: Post-exploitation task-credential theft via IMDS -> cloud pivot
findings.attack_path: On container compromise (e.g., a vulnerable/EOL dependency, TM-018), the task role's temporary credentials are readable from the instance metadata service and usable off-box. Combined with unrestricted egress (TM-020) and PassRole (TM-010), a single container foothold becomes a cloud-account foothold.
findings.remediation: Enforce IMDSv2 (hop limit 1, tokens required) on the tasks; minimize the task role to least privilege (see TM-010); restrict egress (TM-020) so stolen credentials cannot be used off-box; add runtime detection.

findings.title: GitHub PAT in plaintext local Terraform state & pipeline config, with no rotation/revocation lifecycle
findings.attack_path: The long-lived GitHub PAT is persisted unencrypted in local terraform.tfstate on the operator workstation and in the CodePipeline source config (readable via the over-broad DevOps role). Theft yields repository write access — the single trust anchor of the whole supply chain. Absorbs the lifecycle gap (former TM-027): the PAT has no rotation/expiry/revocation, so a leak stays valid indefinitely until a human notices.
findings.remediation: Replace the long-lived PAT with a GitHub App / OIDC federation to CodePipeline (short-lived, fine-grained, auto-rotating) sourced from a managed secret store; move Terraform state to an encrypted remote backend with locking (TM-024); set an expiry and documented revocation path. This single change closes both the storage and lifecycle gaps.

findings.title: main-push auto-deploy to production with no approval gate
findings.attack_path: PollForSourceChanges=true on branch main means any merge/push auto-builds and blue/green-deploys to production with no manual approval, no review gate, no separation of duties. One developer (or a stolen PAT, TM-012) ships arbitrary code straight to prod.
findings.remediation: Add a CodePipeline manual-approval action before Deploy; enforce protected main with required reviews and status checks; require signed commits; separate deploy authority from code authorship.

findings.title: Default AWS-owned encryption only; S3 lacks public-access-block/versioning; force_destroy=true
findings.attack_path: Every store relies on AWS-owned default keys — no CMK, no key-usage audit, no cross-account key isolation. S3 buckets have no public-access-block or versioning and force_destroy=true. Confidentiality/recoverability are the platform default, not deliberate; there is no defense against key-plane/account-plane exposure and no object-version safety net. (Confidentiality/key-management framing; destruction-impact captured separately in TM-026.)
findings.remediation: Enable SSE-KMS with customer-managed keys on S3/DynamoDB/ECR; add S3 public-access-block, versioning, and access logging; enable DynamoDB PITR; remove force_destroy from managed buckets.

findings.title: Privileged CodeBuild (Docker-in-Docker) -> build-time RCE, container/host escape
findings.attack_path: CodeBuild runs with privileged_mode=true. Any code executing during the build — a malicious npm dependency, a poisoned :latest base image (TM-018), or attacker-modified source (TM-013) — runs with privileged Docker access and the build's IAM identity, enabling container/host escape and lateral movement.
findings.remediation: Remove privileged_mode where possible (use a rootless/kaniko/buildkit image builder that does not need Docker-in-Docker); pin and update the CodeBuild image; scope the build IAM identity to least privilege; run dependency/image scanning before the build trusts inputs.

findings.title: Over-permissioned DevOps role (broad ECS/S3 action lists + iam:PassRole * on wildcard resources)
findings.attack_path: The pipeline-assumed DevOps role (R3) grants enumerated S3 write/read actions and an extensive ECS action list (including RegisterTaskDefinition + RunTask) on resources=["*"], plus iam:PassRole on *. ecs:RegisterTaskDefinition + ecs:RunTask + iam:PassRole * is a complete privilege-escalation combo (register a task def with any role and run it) -> account-wide. Compromise of the build (TM-015) inherits this power. (Grants are wildcard-resource, not literal s3:*/ecs:* action wildcards.)
findings.remediation: Scope every DevOps statement to the specific bucket/repo/cluster/service ARNs it needs; constrain iam:PassRole to the exact task/execution role ARNs via an iam:PassedToService condition; remove account-wide resources=["*"] on write/run actions.

findings.title: Mutable ECR tags + no scan-on-push -> silent image replacement
findings.attack_path: ECR repositories are MUTABLE with no scan_on_push. Anyone with ECR push (via the DevOps role, TM-016, or the pipeline, TM-013) can overwrite the deployed tag / :latest; the next task start or scale-out silently pulls the attacker's image. No digest pinning in the task definition to detect it.
findings.remediation: Set image_tag_mutability=IMMUTABLE; enable scan_on_push (or Inspector); deploy tasks by image digest, not floating tag; add image signing (cosign) and verify at deploy.

findings.title: Unpinned :latest base images, no SCA/SBOM, EOL runtime deps -> upstream supply-chain implant
findings.attack_path: Dockerfiles pull bitnami/node:latest and nginx:latest (mutable, unpinned, non-reproducible); there is no dependency or image scanning, no SBOM, no lockfile-integrity gate. Runtime deps are EOL/maintenance (Vue 2, aws-sdk v2). A compromised upstream tag or a known-CVE dependency lands in production unremarked, and is the RCE entry point for KC-04.
findings.remediation: Pin base images by digest; add SCA (npm audit / Dependabot / Snyk) and container image scanning as blocking pipeline gates; generate and store an SBOM; upgrade off EOL Vue 2 and aws-sdk v2 (to v3).

findings.title: Deploy-artifact & task-definition tampering (artifact bucket + build-time sed injects taskRoleArn)
findings.attack_path: buildspec.yml:18 injects a taskRoleArn into taskdef.json via sed, and the build writes taskdef.json/appspec.yaml into the artifact bucket (D3). An attacker who influences the build environment or the artifact bucket (DevOps role S3 write, TM-016) can deploy an attacker-chosen task role or container definition — directly weaponizing PassRole (TM-010/TM-016).
findings.remediation: Treat taskdef/appspec as reviewed, version-controlled artifacts rather than sed-templated at build; restrict artifact-bucket write to the pipeline role only; validate/sign the task definition before deploy; constrain which role ARNs a task definition may reference.

findings.title: Unrestricted egress (SG egress -1 to 0.0.0.0/0, NAT to 0.0.0.0/0) -> exfiltration & C2
findings.attack_path: Tasks may reach any Internet host outbound with no allow-listing or DNS filtering (SG egress -1, NAT 0.0.0.0/0). A compromised container (TM-011/TM-015) has a clear channel to exfiltrate catalog/credentials and reach command-and-control — the amplifier that turns any foothold into data loss.
findings.remediation: Restrict egress security-group rules to required destinations/ports; add VPC endpoints for DynamoDB/S3/ECR/CloudWatch/Logs so service traffic never traverses the Internet; add egress DNS/proxy filtering and flow-log-based anomaly detection.

findings.title: No ALB access logs, VPC flow logs, CloudTrail, GuardDuty, or Config -> no detection or attribution
findings.attack_path: The IaC declares only CloudWatch task/build logs. With no ALB access logs, no VPC flow logs, and no account trail (CloudTrail/GuardDuty/Config), scraping, cost abuse, credential misuse, and deploys are neither detectable nor attributable. Scored as the cross-cutting amplifier under all four kill chains (near-certain undetectability), not a standalone breach; repudiation is total for pipeline/deploy actions.
findings.remediation: Enable ALB access logs, VPC flow logs, org-wide CloudTrail, GuardDuty, and AWS Config; ship to a tamper-resistant log account with retention aligned to forensic need; add alerting on anomalous API/egress/deploy activity.

findings.title: Sensitive data in logs + short retention (console.error(raw err), 30-day)
findings.attack_path: The error handler logs the raw error object to stderr -> CloudWatch. Low sensitivity today (non-PII), but the pattern captures internal detail and 30-day retention limits forensic reach; reading it needs log-read access.
findings.remediation: Log structured, redacted errors (no raw objects); scrub secrets/PII before logging; set retention to the forensic/compliance requirement; restrict log-group read access.

findings.title: Missing client security headers / CSP (Nginx default)
findings.attack_path: The Nginx-served SPA sets no CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, or HSTS. Vue auto-escapes so there is no direct XSS sink today, but the missing headers remove defense-in-depth against clickjacking and against any future injection, and pair with TM-002 (an on-path attacker's injected script faces no CSP).
findings.remediation: Add a strict Content-Security-Policy plus X-Frame-Options=DENY, X-Content-Type-Options=nosniff, Referrer-Policy, and HSTS (with TLS, TM-002) to the Nginx config.

findings.title: Terraform state without remote backend / locking — IaC integrity & inventory exposure
findings.attack_path: State is a local unencrypted file with no locking and no remote backend. Beyond the PAT (TM-012), it holds the full resource inventory; concurrent/interrupted applies can corrupt it (no locking), and there is no access control or audit around it.
findings.remediation: Move state to an encrypted remote backend (S3 + SSE-KMS) with DynamoDB state locking; restrict backend access via IAM; enable versioning on the state bucket for recovery.

findings.title: Single NAT gateway — egress SPOF cascading to full API failure
findings.attack_path: Without VPC endpoints, all task->DynamoDB/S3/ECR/CloudWatch traffic egresses through a single NAT gateway in one AZ. Loss of that AZ/NAT (or targeted NAT exhaustion) breaks the API's dependency calls even though the ALB and a second AZ's tasks survive — the fragile handler (TM-008) then surfaces errors. A bigger blast radius than 'single NAT' suggests.
findings.remediation: Deploy a NAT gateway per AZ, or (better) add VPC gateway/interface endpoints for DynamoDB/S3/ECR/CloudWatch so service traffic bypasses NAT entirely and survives an AZ loss.

findings.title: Irreversible S3 data destruction/ransom (overwrite via PutObject + force_destroy, no versioning)
findings.attack_path: With no versioning on either bucket, an attacker who reaches the DevOps role (via KC-03) can overwrite/ransom objects using s3:PutObject on resources=["*"] (the role has PutObject, not DeleteObject) with no version history to recover from and no detection (TM-021); separately, force_destroy=true lets a compromised or mistaken terraform destroy permanently delete both non-empty buckets. Distinct destruction/availability impact beyond TM-014's confidentiality framing.
findings.remediation: Enable S3 versioning + Object Lock (or MFA-delete) on both buckets; scope DevOps s3:PutObject to the specific bucket ARNs; remove force_destroy from managed buckets; add access logging and deletion/overwrite alarms.

kill_chains.goal: Anonymous economic/availability denial with zero credentials
On-path HTTP interception -> malicious content executed in a victim's browser
CI/CD compromise -> production RCE -> account-wide privilege escalation (composite CRITICAL)
Container foothold -> IMDS credential theft -> cloud privilege escalation & exfiltration
